name: HPV Vaccination Coverage and Policy Implementation
anchorClaim: HPV vaccination coverage among university-age and catch-up-eligible populations remains below public-health targets and varies by at least [X] percentage points between the highest and lowest coverage regions, as documented in epidemiological surveillance and policy-implementation studies.
plainQuestion: HPV vaccination coverage among university-age and catch-up-eligible populations falls short of public-health targets, and varies widely from one region to another.
confidenceSummary: The Grade F is a caution about quality: the studies support the general picture that coverage falls short of target rather than the specific size of the gap, and most rest on brief summaries rather than full papers.
dataQualityNote: All 196 records were pulled from the anchor's real datom_ids list. A GSI query on this anchor's own datomerId (ce304af2...) returned zero rows because the underlying extracted-datom records instead carry seven distinct job-level datomerId values: 465f748a-1fce-4f97-9add-3284fc028643 groups the plurality at 94 of 196 (48%), 27763aa0-7e51-4648-b500-95d95bcd73bd groups 58 (30%), and five smaller groups cover the remaining 44; get-item/batch-get-item on the 196 listed datom_ids was used instead and returned all 196 with no gaps or missing records. 133 of 196 records (68%) are abstract-only TEXT_NO_METADATA extractions rather than full-text PDFs, methodology is described using 123 distinct free-text labels (79 of them singletons), 15 records lack a DOI, 3 lack listed authors, and all 196 records carry review status PENDING (not yet reviewer-verified). The anchor claim itself contains an unfilled "[X] percentage points" placeholder, so no single validated magnitude for the coverage gap exists in the underlying data.

guide.whatScienceSays: DATOM looked at 45 studies that directly tested this claim. All 45 support the idea that HPV vaccination coverage among university-age and catch-up-eligible groups falls short of public-health targets and varies widely from region to region; none pointed the other way. So the clear findings back the claim, which is what the "Supported" verdict below means. But the Grade F beside it matters just as much: the evidence is weak in quality even though it points one way, so treat this as the current direction, not a settled, high-certainty result. Many more studies touched on the topic without testing this exact claim; they appear further down, tagged by what they looked at.
guide.howConfident:
DATOM gives this claim a confidence score of 20 out of 100, which we call Speculative. That's true even though 74% of the 196 sources point the same direction and none disagree with it. That's a big gap between how much the sources agree and how confident the score is.

Here's why: the confidence score isn't about whether studies agree on the general idea. It's about whether the evidence can back up one specific, citable number. This claim has a blank spot built into it: it talks about an "[X] percentage point" gap in coverage, but no study here, and no combination of them, has produced one agreed number to fill that blank.

The way the studies were done makes this worse. Across only 196 sources, there are 123 different ways the methods were described, and 79 of those descriptions are each used only once. That means a Belgian disease-spread model, a US insurance-claims study, and a Rhode Island survey are all being counted as evidence for the same claim. But they were built in completely different ways, and several of them didn't report how many people or samples they studied.

On top of that, 133 of the 196 sources (68%) are based only on abstracts, the short summary of a study, rather than the full published paper. That limits how much of each study's actual method DATOM could check. And all 196 sources are still waiting for a human reviewer to check them; none has been verified yet.

Strong agreement on direction, combined with an unanswered core question and evidence that hasn't been checked yet, is exactly the pattern that produces a low confidence score even when the support percentage looks high.
decisionSupport: Don't quote one single national number for the coverage gap. The claim's own "[X] percentage point" blank was never filled in. And the two clearest regional findings in our sources don't even agree on scale: Belgium shows a 54 to 61 point gap (about 90% coverage in Flanders versus 29 to 36% in Wallonia-Brussels), while France's national full-course rate is flat at 18.6%, less than a third of its own 60% target.

If you're using this for outreach or policy, split people by whether they're in the "catch-up" age group, not just by age alone. A US study of 118 million people with commercial insurance found that uptake among the 22-and-older catch-up group had dropped to 1% or less by 2016. That's not a sign of a new access problem. It's because teens are now getting vaccinated earlier, so fewer people need catching up later.

Treat coverage numbers from different studies as pointing in the same general direction, but don't average them together as if they measured the same thing. The methods behind the 196 sources were described in 123 different ways, 79 of which show up only once. They include disease-spread models, insurance-claims analyses, and one-time surveys, none of which were designed to be combined.

Give more weight to findings backed by a full published study rather than just a summary. 133 of the 196 sources (68%) are based only on the abstract, the short summary at the top of a paper, not the full paper itself. That means a good chunk of the 74% support figure rests on summary-level claims rather than a fully checked method.

Before citing any specific percentage from this claim in something high-stakes, flag it for a human reviewer to double check first. All 196 sources are still waiting for that review. On top of that, 15 sources are missing a DOI (a permanent link or ID for the study) and 3 don't list any authors, so we haven't fully confirmed where all of this evidence came from yet.
guide.faultLines:
There are three real weak spots in this evidence.

The Gap Size Was Never Pinned Down: the claim asks for one specific percentage-point number to fill in its "[X]" blank. But the 196 sources only support the general idea, that coverage is below target and varies by region, not any single agreed number. So the 74% support figure is really answering an easier question than the one the claim is actually asking.

No Two Studies Used the Same Method: the methods behind the 196 sources are described in 123 different ways, 79 of which appear only once. Several of the most solid supporting studies, including the ones from Belgium, Switzerland, and Rhode Island, simply list sample size as "Not reported." That makes it impossible to know how much weight each study's result actually deserves.

We Haven't Checked Everything Yet: 68% of the sources (133 of 196) are based only on abstracts rather than the full published study. All 196 are still waiting on human review. 15 are missing a DOI (a permanent study identifier), and 3 don't list any authors. On top of that, the sources span publication years 2011 to 2026, but 30% of them (59 of 196) were published in just 2025 and 2026 alone. That means the newest surveillance data is counted much more heavily than the older studies it's being lumped in with.

datoms.claim: Regional HPV vaccination coverage in Belgium varies by at least 54-61 percentage points between the highest coverage region (Flanders at 90%) and the lowest coverage region (Wallonia-Brussels at 29-36%).
datoms.source: S. Simoens, A. Bento-Abreu, B. Merckx, S. Joubert, Steve Vermeersch "Health Impact and Cost-Effectiveness of Implementing Gender-Neutral Vaccination With the 9-Valent Human Papillomavirus Vaccine in Belgium" (2021). doi:10.3389/fphar.2021.628434
datoms.population: School-aged children in Flanders (11-12 years) and Wallonia-Brussels (12-13 years) regions, Belgium
datoms.measure: Regional variation in HPV vaccine coverage rate (percentage points)
datoms.methodology: Mathematical transmission dynamic model with epidemiological surveillance data
datoms.notes: The substantial regional variation in coverage reflects differences in program implementation, regional governance structures, and vaccine types used. The paper uses these documented regional differences as key parameters in modeling cost-effectiveness of gender-neutral vaccination strategies. Limitations: The study reports coverage at specific time points rather than continuous data. The analysis does not fully explore the reasons for regional variation. Catch-up program coverage was projected (50%) rather than observed.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies substantially across European regions, with differences of at least several percentage points between highest and lowest coverage areas.
datoms.source: Ngoc-Ha Nguyen-Huu, Nathalie Thilly, Tarik Derrough, Emmanouela Sdona, Frédérique Claudot "Human papillomavirus vaccination coverage, policies, and practical implementation across Europe" (2019). doi:10.1016/j.vaccine.2019.11.081
datoms.population: University-age and catch-up-eligible populations across European countries
datoms.domain: Public health epidemiology and vaccination policy
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage by region
datoms.methodology: Epidemiological surveillance and policy review
datoms.notes: Regional variation in HPV vaccination coverage reflects differences in national policies, healthcare infrastructure, and implementation strategies across Europe. Limitations: Data availability and comparability across countries may vary; some regions may have incomplete surveillance data.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies substantially by age group, with adolescents aged 15–17 years demonstrating higher series completion rates than adolescents aged 13–14 years across all survey years.
datoms.source: Taylor Mullin, Jesse Plascak, Alai Tan, Jodi Ford, Henry Duah "Trends in HPV vaccination initiation and completion among U.S. adolescents aged 13-17 years, 2021-2023: Findings from the National Immunization Survey-Teen." (2026). doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0349299
datoms.population: U.S. adolescents aged 13–17 years stratified by age group (13–14 and 15–17 years)
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination series completion rate by age group (%)
datoms.methodology: Repeated cross-sectional survey analysis with provider-verified vaccination records
datoms.notes: Age-related trends provide insight into opportunities for improvement. Older adolescents (15–17 years) exhibited higher completion rates, likely reflecting increased time since vaccine eligibility and additional opportunities for healthcare encounters. However, delaying initiation until mid-adolescence leaves less time to complete the series before the onset of sexual activity. Limitations: Only three years of data analyzed. Study was descriptive and did not examine sociodemographic or contextual predictors beyond age and sex. Immunocompromised status could not be identified in public-use files.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage in France remains substantially below the 60% public-health target set by the French Cancer Plan 2014-2019, with full-scheme coverage at 18.6% among 11-14 year-old girls by 2018.
datoms.source: F. Dalon, L. Majed, M. Belhassen, F. Jacoud, M. Berard "PIN103 Trends in Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Vaccine Coverage Rates (VCR) in France: A French Claims DATA Study" (2020). doi:10.1016/j.jval.2020.08.944
datoms.population: Girls aged 11-16 years in France who initiated HPV vaccination 2016-2018
datoms.measure: HPV vaccine full-scheme cumulative coverage rate (percentage)
datoms.methodology: Claims database analysis with cumulative coverage rate estimation
datoms.notes: HPV vaccine coverage rates significantly increased between 2016 and 2018, providing positive signs regarding resumption of vaccination. However, the absolute coverage levels remain far below the 60% target. Limitations: The study covers only 2016-2018 data; longitudinal follow-up until 2022 was planned. A potential impact of COVID-19 lockdown on VCR could be expected but was not assessed.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination uptake among catch-up-eligible populations (ages 16–26) declined substantially over the study period, from peak uptake in 2007 (when vaccine became available) to ≤1% by 2016 among those aged 22 and older.
datoms.source: V. Prabhu, N. Bansal, Zhiwen Liu, Rodney Finalle, M. Sénécal "HPV vaccination uptake and administration from 2006 to 2016 in a commercially insured population of the United States" (2020). doi:10.1186/s12889-021-11664-1
datoms.population: Commercially insured 9- to 26-year-olds in the United States, 2006–2016
datoms.measure: Annual HPV vaccination uptake in catch-up-eligible age groups (16–26 years)
datoms.methodology: Retrospective claims database analysis
datoms.notes: Authors note that 'over time, more and more teenagers were vaccinated at younger ages which means less were available for vaccination as older adolescents and young adults,' explaining the decline in catch-up uptake. This reflects a cohort effect rather than increased uptake in older age groups. Limitations: Limited to commercially insured population. Only birth year available, not exact age. Vaccines not submitted for reimbursement not captured.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage among adolescents in Switzerland varies between regions, with documented differences in coverage rates across the study period 2008–2022.
datoms.source: Vasiliki Baroutsou, Monica Wymann, Anne Spaar Zographos, Kyra Zens, Jan Fehr "Human papillomavirus vaccine uptake and the impact of school-based health services in Switzerland: a cross-sectional study." (2026). doi:10.1136/bmjph-2025-004208
datoms.population: Adolescents in Switzerland
datoms.domain: Epidemiology and public health vaccination surveillance
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage and schedule completion rates by region and delivery method
datoms.methodology: Cross-sectional study with temporal trend analysis
datoms.notes: The study assessed differences in vaccination outcomes by delivery through school health services, suggesting that delivery method may influence coverage rates. Limitations: The abstract does not report specific limitations; full-text limitations are not provided.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage among Australian women aged 18-26 years remains below public-health targets, with only 55.2% receiving dose 1 and 31.7% completing the full three-dose series.
datoms.source: J. Brotherton, D. Gertig, Genevieve Chappell, L. Rowlands, M. Saville "Catching up with the catch-up: HPV vaccination coverage data for Australian women aged 18-26 years from the National HPV Vaccination Program Register." (2011). doi:10.33321/cdi.2011.35.18
datoms.population: Australian women aged 18-26 years participating in the National HPV Vaccination Program catch-up campaign
datoms.domain: Epidemiological surveillance and public health policy implementation
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage (dose 1, 2, and 3 completion rates)
datoms.methodology: Cross-sectional analysis of vaccination register notifications
datoms.sample_size: 1.7 million vaccine doses for women aged 18-26 years
datoms.notes: The authors conclude that over half of Australian women aged 18-26 years commenced HPV vaccine courses and about one-third are fully vaccinated, indicating substantial gaps in coverage. Limitations: Some of the differences in coverage observed between states and territories likely reflect differing notification mechanisms rather than true differences in vaccination uptake.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies by geographic region or demographic subgroup within Rhode Island, indicating unequal distribution of vaccination uptake.
datoms.source: Hyun Hanna Kim, Tricia Washburn, Kathy Marceau, Patricia Raymond "Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Vaccination Coverage among Rhode Island Adolescents, 2008-2014." (2016)
datoms.population: Rhode Island adolescents aged 11-18 years, stratified by region or demographic characteristics
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage by region or demographic subgroup
datoms.methodology: Epidemiological surveillance study with stratified analysis
datoms.notes: Regional and demographic disparities in HPV vaccination coverage suggest the need for targeted public health efforts to improve coverage in underserved areas. Limitations: Study limited to Rhode Island; specific magnitude of regional variation not detailed in available abstract.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies between Australian regions, with regional differences in uptake among female adolescents in the school-based program.
datoms.source: J. Brotherton, S. L. Murray, Madeline Hall, L. Andrewartha, Carolyn Banks "Human papillomavirus vaccine coverage among female Australian adolescents: success of the school‐based approach" (2013). doi:10.5694/mja13.10272
datoms.population: Female Australian adolescents in school-based HPV vaccination program
datoms.measure: Regional variation in HPV vaccination coverage
datoms.methodology: Epidemiological surveillance study
datoms.notes: The identification of regional variation suggests that while the school-based approach was generally successful, coverage was not uniform across all regions, indicating potential for targeted interventions in lower-coverage areas. Limitations: Specific limitations regarding regional data collection not detailed in provided excerpt.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies across U.S. states and jurisdictions, with states having school-entry or education mandates not achieving higher coverage than states without such mandates during 2009–2013.
datoms.source: Rebecca B. Perkins, Meng‐Yun Lin, Sherrie Flynt Wallington, Amresh Hanchate "Impact of school-entry and education mandates by states on HPV vaccination coverage: Analysis of the 2009–2013 National Immunization Survey-Teen" (2016). doi:10.1080/21645515.2016.1150394
datoms.population: Girls ages 13–17 residing in U.S. states and jurisdictions
datoms.measure: HPV vaccine series initiation and completion coverage by state mandate status
datoms.methodology: Multilevel logistic regression analysis of national survey data
datoms.notes: The authors conclude that existing school-entry and education mandates have not increased HPV vaccination coverage, likely because liberal opt-out provisions in school-entry mandates weaken their impact. Policy-makers should be aware of these limitations when considering vaccination legislation. Limitations: The study does not report specific percentage-point differences between highest and lowest coverage regions, limiting quantification of the variation magnitude. Cross-sectional design prevents causal inference about mandate effectiveness over time.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies significantly by urban/rural residence, with urban residents having substantially higher initiation rates than rural residents.
datoms.source: C. Macander, Hui Wang, M. Galafassi, Graham M Jones, Antara Das "Role of Race, Rurality, and Age in Human Papillomavirus Vaccine Initiation among US Women" (2025). doi:10.14423/SMJ.0000000000001813
datoms.population: Adult females aged 18 to 43 years in the United States, stratified by urban/rural residence
datoms.domain: Epidemiology; Vaccine coverage surveillance; Health disparities
datoms.measure: HPV vaccine initiation by urban/rural classification
datoms.methodology: Cross-sectional survey analysis with logistic regression
datoms.notes: The authors recommend that efforts to increase HPV vaccine uptake should focus on rural communities, acknowledging rural residence as a barrier to vaccination. Limitations: Not explicitly stated in the provided text.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies by geographic area within Chengdu, with stratified analysis showing differences across regions.
datoms.source: Jing Li, Dandan Zhao, Tongtong Zi, Rongna Huang, Fan Zhao "Evolving trends in HPV vaccination coverage among women aged 9–45 in Chengdu, China: insights from 2017 to 2023" (2025). doi:10.1016/j.vaccine.2025.127579
datoms.population: Females aged 9-45 years in Chengdu, China
datoms.domain: Epidemiology and public health vaccination surveillance
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage stratified by geographic area
datoms.methodology: Descriptive epidemiological surveillance analysis stratified by geographic area
datoms.notes: The paper acknowledges that vaccination rates vary by geographic area but does not provide specific quantitative comparisons between the highest and lowest coverage regions. Limitations: The paper stratifies by geographic area but does not report the specific percentage-point range of variation between highest and lowest coverage regions, limiting direct quantification of regional disparities.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage in the Wallonia-Brussels region of Belgium is substantially lower than in Flanders, at approximately 29-36% depending on time since program initiation.
datoms.source: S. Simoens, A. Bento-Abreu, B. Merckx, S. Joubert, Steve Vermeersch "Health Impact and Cost-Effectiveness of Implementing Gender-Neutral Vaccination With the 9-Valent Human Papillomavirus Vaccine in Belgium" (2021). doi:10.3389/fphar.2021.628434
datoms.population: School-aged children (12-13 years) in Wallonia-Brussels region, Belgium
datoms.measure: HPV vaccine coverage rate (%)
datoms.methodology: Mathematical transmission dynamic model with epidemiological surveillance data
datoms.notes: The lower uptake in Wallonia-Brussels compared to Flanders reflects differences in program implementation and regional factors. The paper notes this regional variation as a key parameter in modeling the cost-effectiveness of gender-neutral vaccination strategies. Limitations: The study reports uptake rates at specific time points (1-2 years and 5-6 years) rather than continuous coverage data. The reasons for lower uptake in Wallonia-Brussels are not detailed in the paper.

datoms.claim: Male HPV vaccination coverage in Australia's school-based program in 2013 shows variation across regions or demographic groups.
datoms.source: Julia Brotherton, Michael Batchelor, Michelle O Bradley, Scott A. Brown, Simone M Duncombe "Interim estimates of male human papillomavirus vaccination coverage in the school-based program in Australia" (2015). doi:10.33321/cdi.2015.39.17
datoms.population: School-age males in Australia eligible for HPV vaccination in 2013
datoms.measure: Male HPV vaccination coverage by region or demographic group
datoms.methodology: Epidemiological surveillance study
datoms.notes: The authors present interim coverage data from the newly extended male HPV vaccination program in Australia's school-based setting. Limitations: The paper provides interim estimates only, suggesting data collection was ongoing and final coverage figures were not yet available.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage among adolescents aged 13–17 years remains below public-health targets, with overall coverage reaching 74.9% before age 18 years.
datoms.source: S. Meyer, David Nmn Yankey, Laurie D. Elam-Evans, S. Pingali, Shannon Stokley "P-5. Human Papillomavirus Vaccination Coverage Among Girls and Boys in the United States: A Birth Year Cohort Analysis of the National Immunization Survey-Teen, 2016–2022" (2025). doi:10.1093/ofid/ofae631.216
datoms.population: Adolescents born 1999–2009 in the United States
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage (cumulative coverage from age 13 to 17 years)
datoms.methodology: Birth cohort analysis using National Immunization Survey-Teen
datoms.notes: Coverage with on-time HPV vaccination and HPV up to date increased by birth cohort among adolescents born 1999–2009 but remains suboptimal. Low uptake increases risk for HPV cancers. Limitations: The study analyzed data from 2016 to 2022 and focused on birth cohorts 1999–2009, which may not reflect current vaccination patterns. NIS-Teen is a telephone survey which may have response bias.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage in the Flanders region of Belgium reaches approximately 90% for both two- and three-dose schedules.
datoms.source: S. Simoens, A. Bento-Abreu, B. Merckx, S. Joubert, Steve Vermeersch "Health Impact and Cost-Effectiveness of Implementing Gender-Neutral Vaccination With the 9-Valent Human Papillomavirus Vaccine in Belgium" (2021). doi:10.3389/fphar.2021.628434
datoms.population: School-aged children (11-12 years) in Flanders region, Belgium
datoms.measure: HPV vaccine coverage rate (%)
datoms.methodology: Mathematical transmission dynamic model with epidemiological surveillance data
datoms.notes: The substantial difference in coverage between regions (90% in Flanders vs. 29-36% in Wallonia-Brussels) reflects regional program implementation differences and demonstrates the geographic variation in vaccination coverage documented in the nucleus claim. Limitations: The study used projected coverage rates for catch-up programs (50% for males and females) based on 10-15 year projections rather than observed data. Regional differences in vaccine types (9vHPV in Flanders vs. 2vHPV in Wallonia-Brussels initially) complicate direct comparison.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies substantially between regions, with school-based programmes achieving 77.2% to 96.1% coverage across different countries (Peru, Uganda, Viet Nam, India).
datoms.source: D. Scott LaMontagne, Sandhya Barge, Nga Thi Le, Emmanuel Mugisha, Mary E. Penny "Human papillomavirus vaccine delivery strategies that achieved high coverage in low- and middle-income countries" (2011). doi:10.2471/blt.11.089862
datoms.population: Adolescent girls in demonstration project areas in India, Peru, Uganda, and Viet Nam; parents or guardians interviewed (n>7000)
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage (full vaccination defined as receipt of all three vaccine doses)
datoms.methodology: Two-stage cluster sample survey
datoms.sample_size: Over 7,000 parents or guardians of adolescent girls
datoms.notes: High coverage with HPV vaccine among young adolescent girls was achieved through various delivery strategies in the developing countries studied. Reinforcing positive motivators for vaccine acceptance is likely to facilitate uptake. Limitations: Not reported

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies significantly by demographic characteristics (age, race/ethnicity, marital status, employment, residency status) among university-age populations.
datoms.source: M. Ward, Terri L. Shill, Yeil Kwon, Mai Dao, Tabitha S. Gillis "HPV vaccination rates and knowledge among students at a University in Kansas" (2026). doi:10.1186/s12982-026-02074-y
datoms.population: Undergraduate and graduate students at a large Midwestern university in Kansas
datoms.domain: Public health epidemiology; HPV vaccination surveillance
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage by demographic subgroups
datoms.methodology: Cross-sectional descriptive survey with chi-square analysis
datoms.notes: Disparities persist across demographic groups, particularly by age and race. These findings underscore the need for campus-based, equitable educational interventions that address structural barriers and promote informed decision-making. Limitations: Study limited to a single university; cross-sectional design; self-reported vaccination status not verified.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage among 10-14 year old girls varies by at least 11 percentage points between the highest and lowest coverage regions in Zimbabwe.
datoms.source: D. Scott LaMontagne, Portia Manangazira, Joan Marembo, Colline Chigodo, Coscar Zvamashakwe "HPV vaccination coverage in three districts in Zimbabwe following national introduction of 0,12 month schedule among 10 to 14 year old girls" (2021). doi:10.1016/j.vaccine.2021.07.012
datoms.population: Girls aged 11-15 years eligible for national HPV vaccination program in three districts of Zimbabwe
datoms.methodology: Population-based two-stage cluster survey
datoms.measure: Two-dose HPV vaccination coverage by district
datoms.notes: Zimbabwe demonstrated that high uptake and successful completion of 2-dose HPV vaccination can be achieved with an annual dosing schedule. Future efforts will focus on minimizing dropout between doses and routinizing annual vaccinations in schools for every subsequent new cohort of eligible girls. Limitations: Challenges assessing ages of girls at schools prior to vaccination; 9% of girls vaccinated were less than 10 years old at time of dose 1.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage in women aged 15–55 years not included in systematic vaccination programmes in Spain remains very low, with cumulative coverage of approximately 4.03% in 2020.
datoms.source: Mar Ramírez, Jesús de la Fuente, Daniel Andı́a, Juan José Guardia Hernández, Gabriel Fiol "HPV vaccination coverage in women between 15 and 55 years old in Spain: Temporal trend during the period 2007–2020" (2021). doi:10.1002/ijgo.14067
datoms.population: Women aged 15–55 years in Spain not included in systematic vaccination programmes
datoms.domain: Epidemiological surveillance and public health policy
datoms.measure: Cumulative HPV vaccination coverage (aVCR) expressed as percentage
datoms.methodology: Temporal trend analysis of surveillance data
datoms.notes: The authors conclude that cumulative HPV vaccination coverage in this catch-up-eligible population remains very low despite a slight upward trend in recent years. COVID-19 did not significantly worsen coverage in 2020. Limitations: The study does not report regional variation in coverage, which is a component of the nucleus claim regarding variation between highest and lowest coverage regions.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies by at least 55 percentage points between the highest and lowest coverage regions in Belgium, with Flanders at 91% and Walloon Region at 36%.
datoms.source: Waa Tjalma, C Brasseur, Tuyet Nha n CHU N G, Nathalie Ribesse, I. Morales "HPV vaccination coverage in the federal state of Belgium according to regions and their impact." (2018)
datoms.population: HPV-vaccinated cohorts in Belgium by region
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage percentage by region
datoms.methodology: Epidemiological surveillance and regional coverage assessment
datoms.notes: The regional difference in coverage represents a real-life case study of disparate vaccination outcomes. Authors note the worst-case scenario could result in one half of the country experiencing proportionally more HPV-related cancers than the other half. Limitations: Study does not provide detailed breakdown by age cohorts within university-age or catch-up-eligible populations specifically; regional-level aggregation masks potential within-region variation.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies by region, with higher hesitancy documented in the Southeast/Mid-Atlantic compared to the Northeast United States.
datoms.source: Andrew Porter, S. Cooper, Aisha King, Carmen Presti, Ingrid V. Williams "Regional voices, different choices: Parents' and caregivers' HPV vaccine attitudes in the northeast and Southeast United States." (2025). doi:10.1016/j.vaccine.2025.127864
datoms.population: Caregivers of children aged 9-17 in the Northeast and Southeast/Mid-Atlantic U.S.
datoms.measure: HPV vaccine hesitancy by region (Southeast/Mid-Atlantic vs. Northeast)
datoms.methodology: Cross-sectional online survey with chi-squared analysis
datoms.notes: HPV vaccine hesitancy is shaped by intersecting identities and regional contexts. Future interventions must address mistrust and misinformation, especially in the Southeast/Mid-Atlantic region. Limitations: The study measured hesitancy attitudes rather than actual vaccination coverage rates; the paper does not report the specific percentage-point difference between regions or coverage among university-age populations.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage in the catch-up cohort (those under age 18) is 66%, which is below the routine cohort coverage of over 90% annually.
datoms.source: K. Kavanagh, K. Pollock, A. Potts, J. Love, K. Cuschieri "Introduction and sustained high coverage of the HPV bivalent vaccine leads to a reduction in prevalence of HPV 16/18 and closely related HPV types" (2014). doi:10.1038/bjc.2014.198
datoms.population: Scottish females aged 12–13 (routine cohort) and under 18 (catch-up cohort)
datoms.measure: Three-dose HPV bivalent vaccine uptake coverage by cohort
datoms.methodology: National immunisation programme surveillance
datoms.notes: The authors note that high vaccine uptake in the routine cohort (>90%) has been achieved and sustained, but the catch-up cohort shows lower overall uptake at 66%, indicating differential coverage between populations. Limitations: The paper does not report regional variation in coverage or provide data on whether coverage meets specific public-health targets. The catch-up cohort figure represents overall uptake without regional breakdown.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies by state, with ≥1-dose coverage among females ranging from 47.8% in Mississippi to 90.1% in Rhode Island, a difference of 42.3 percentage points.
datoms.source: Tanja Y. Walker, Laurie D. Elam-Evans, J. Singleton, D. Yankey, L. Markowitz "National, Regional, State, and Selected Local Area Vaccination Coverage Among Adolescents Aged 13–17 Years — United States, 2016" (2017). doi:10.15585/mmwr.mm6633a2
datoms.population: Female adolescents aged 13-17 years across U.S. states
datoms.domain: Epidemiological surveillance and state-level vaccination coverage variation
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage (≥1 dose) by state
datoms.methodology: National survey with state-level stratification
datoms.sample_size: 9,661 female adolescents across 50 states and selected local areas
datoms.notes: The authors note that vaccination coverage varied substantially by state and that during 2013-2016, the greatest statistically significant average annual increases in ≥1-dose HPV vaccination coverage were in New York City (7.7 percentage points), Nevada (7.6), Maryland (7.4), Guam (7.3), New York (7.2), and Alaska (7.1). Limitations: State-level estimates may have wider confidence intervals for smaller populations. The paper does not provide detailed analysis of state-level policy or programmatic factors driving these differences.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies substantially by geographic region, with a 15.4 percentage point difference between non-MSA and MSA principal city areas for up-to-date status.
datoms.source: Tanja Y. Walker, Laurie D. Elam–Evans, David Yankey, Lauri E. Markowitz, Charnetta Williams "National, Regional, State, and Selected Local Area Vaccination Coverage Among Adolescents Aged 13–17 Years — United States, 2018" (2019). doi:10.15585/mmwr.mm6833a2
datoms.population: Adolescents aged 13–17 years stratified by MSA status (non-MSA n=3,593; MSA nonprincipal city n=7,543; MSA principal city n=7,564)
datoms.domain: Epidemiological surveillance and geographic disparities in immunization
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage by geographic region (metropolitan statistical area status)
datoms.methodology: National cross-sectional survey stratified by metropolitan statistical area
datoms.notes: The disparity in HPV vaccination coverage by MSA status is not well understood; however, lower prevalence of provider recommendations in non-MSA areas might be a factor. Efforts to ensure rural health care providers have resources and training to educate parents about HPV vaccination benefits may increase coverage. Limitations: Estimates stratified by jurisdiction might be unreliable because of small sample sizes. The disparity mechanism is not fully understood.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage among teens aged 13-17 varies by rural-urban residence, with girls from isolated small rural towns showing lower initiation (51.0%) and completion (30.0%) rates compared to urban girls (56.0% and 35.9% respectively).
datoms.source: Allison L. Swiecki‐Sikora, Kevin Henry, Deanna Kepka "HPV Vaccination Coverage Among US Teens Across the Rural‐Urban Continuum" (2019). doi:10.1111/jrh.12353
datoms.population: US teens aged 13-17 years stratified by rural-urban residence
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination initiation (≥1 dose) and completion (≥3 doses) rates by geographic region
datoms.methodology: Cross-sectional survey analysis with logistic regression
datoms.notes: Rural residence is associated with lower HPV vaccination coverage among both girls and boys. Geographic disparities in vaccination uptake may reflect differences in healthcare access, provider recommendations, or community attitudes toward vaccination. Limitations: Cross-sectional design limits causal inference. Data from 2012-2013 may not reflect current coverage. ZIP code-based classification may not perfectly capture individual rural-urban status.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies substantially across US states, with measurable differences between highest and lowest coverage regions among young women.
datoms.source: Chenxi Jiang, Philip S Rosenberg, Jessica Star, Priti Bandi, Robert A Bednarczyk "State-level progress in reducing cervical cancer incidence among US young women between the pre- and post-human papillomavirus vaccination eras." (2026). doi:10.1093/jnci/djag051
datoms.population: US young women in the pre- and post-HPV vaccination eras
datoms.measure: State-level cervical cancer incidence and HPV vaccination coverage variation
datoms.methodology: Epidemiological surveillance analysis
datoms.notes: The authors note that while HPV vaccination has produced measurable national benefits, understanding state-level variation is important for public health policy and implementation assessment. Limitations: State-level data characterization remains incomplete; the abstract does not provide specific quantitative variation metrics between highest and lowest coverage regions.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage among adolescents aged 13-17 years in 2017 was 65.5% for ≥1 dose initiation, remaining below the public-health target of higher coverage.
datoms.source: Tanja Y. Walker, Laurie D. Elam-Evans, D. Yankey, Lauri E. Markowitz, Charnetta Williams "National, Regional, State, and Selected Local Area Vaccination Coverage Among Adolescents Aged 13–17 Years — United States, 2017" (2018). doi:10.15585/mmwr.mm6733a1
datoms.population: Adolescents aged 13-17 years in the United States (N=20,949; 47% female, 53% male)
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage (≥1 dose and up-to-date status)
datoms.methodology: National cross-sectional survey with provider-reported vaccination histories
datoms.notes: HPV vaccination initiation remains lower than coverage with MenACWY and Tdap, suggesting ongoing challenges to providing all three vaccines during the same visit. The 5.1 percentage point annual increase in series initiation since 2013 is encouraging, but efforts are needed to target unvaccinated teens and eliminate missed vaccination opportunities. Limitations: Overall household response rate was 25.7%; only 53.6% of landline and 47.1% of cell phone interviews included adequate provider data. Estimates stratified by state/local area might be unreliable due to small sample sizes. NIS-Teen includes only adolescents aged 13-17 years, potentially underestimating coverage for vaccines received at age ≥18 years.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination initiation coverage varies substantially by state, with 18 states achieving ≥80% initiation by 2023 while Southern states lagged behind.
datoms.source: Victor I. Agboli, Idowu A. Usman, Abdulazeez Alabi, Tope Amusa "Trends and disparities in HPV vaccination among U.S. adolescents, 2018–2023" (2025). doi:10.1515/ohe-2025-0073
datoms.population: U.S. adolescents aged 13–17 across states
datoms.measure: HPV vaccine initiation coverage by state
datoms.methodology: National survey with provider verification and state-level stratification
datoms.notes: Best practices for improving HPV vaccination include strengthening vaccination infrastructure in low-performing Southern states and replicating high-performing regional models. Limitations: Not explicitly stated in abstract or results section provided.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies substantially by geographic region, with ≥1-dose coverage ranging from 46.9% in Wyoming to 91.9% in District of Columbia, a difference of 45.0 percentage points.
datoms.source: Tanja Y. Walker, Laurie D. Elam-Evans, D. Yankey, Lauri E. Markowitz, Charnetta Williams "National, Regional, State, and Selected Local Area Vaccination Coverage Among Adolescents Aged 13–17 Years — United States, 2017" (2018). doi:10.15585/mmwr.mm6733a1
datoms.population: Adolescents aged 13-17 years across 50 U.S. states, District of Columbia, selected local areas, and territories (N=20,949)
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage (≥1 dose) by state and local jurisdiction
datoms.methodology: National cross-sectional survey with state and local area stratification
datoms.notes: The paper notes that HPV vaccination coverage varies by jurisdiction and identifies disparities by metropolitan statistical area status, with rural (non-MSA) areas showing lower coverage than urban areas. Rural residents are less likely to have knowledge of HPV vaccine and its importance in cancer prevention. Limitations: Estimates stratified by state/local area might be unreliable because of small sample sizes. Multiple statistical tests were conducted, and a small number might be significant by chance alone.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies by geographic region, with a difference of 9.6 percentage points for ≥1 dose and 9.8 percentage points for up-to-date status between non-MSA and MSA principal city areas among adolescents at or above the poverty level.
datoms.source: Laurie D. Elam–Evans, David Yankey, James A. Singleton, Natalie Sterrett, Lauri E. Markowitz "National, Regional, State, and Selected Local Area Vaccination Coverage Among Adolescents Aged 13–17 Years — United States, 2019" (2020). doi:10.15585/mmwr.mm6933a1
datoms.population: Adolescents aged 13–17 years at or above the poverty level in non-MSA and MSA principal city areas (N = 8,649)
datoms.domain: Epidemiological surveillance and geographic health disparities
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage by metropolitan statistical area status
datoms.methodology: National cross-sectional survey with stratified geographic analysis
datoms.sample_size: 8,649 adolescents at or above poverty level
datoms.notes: The authors note that geographic disparities among higher socioeconomic status adolescents may indicate lower vaccine confidence in non-MSA areas. The lack of disparity among lower-income adolescents may reflect access to the Vaccines for Children program. Limitations: Response rate was 19.7% overall, with only 44.0% of households having adequate provider data. Bias may remain despite adjustments for nonresponse and noncoverage.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage among university students varies across geographic regions, with disparities documented between different areas.
datoms.source: Yunjun Yan, Shuang Guan, Wei Chen, Junli Shi, Ruoyu Chao "Trends, disparities, and multilevel interventions: A global review of HPV vaccination among university students." (2026). doi:10.1080/21645515.2026.2667395
datoms.population: University students worldwide
datoms.measure: Geographic variation in HPV vaccination coverage
datoms.methodology: Systematic review and synthesis
datoms.notes: The review identifies geographic disparities as a key finding but does not provide specific quantitative thresholds for the percentage-point variation between regions. Limitations: The review acknowledges disparities exist but does not specify the magnitude of regional variation in percentage points, which is a specific constraint of the nucleus claim.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies by state, with provider recommendation prevalence ranging from 59.5% to 90.7% across states, representing a 31.2 percentage point variation.
datoms.source: Tanja Y. Walker, Laurie D. Elam–Evans, David Yankey, Lauri E. Markowitz, Charnetta Williams "National, Regional, State, and Selected Local Area Vaccination Coverage Among Adolescents Aged 13–17 Years — United States, 2018" (2019). doi:10.15585/mmwr.mm6833a2
datoms.population: Parents/guardians of adolescents aged 13–17 years across all U.S. states
datoms.domain: Epidemiological surveillance and provider communication patterns
datoms.measure: Prevalence of parental report of provider recommendation for HPV vaccination by state
datoms.methodology: National survey with state-level stratification of provider recommendation prevalence
datoms.notes: Provider recommendation continues to be a strong predictor of HPV vaccination. However, even when a provider recommendation was given, only 75% accepted the vaccine, suggesting other barriers exist. Equipping providers with tools to give strong recommendations is a priority, especially in states where recommendations were less commonly reported. Limitations: Provider recommendation variable is based on parental recall and thus subject to recall bias.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies substantially between different populations in high-income countries, with adolescent girls at 67.75%, adolescent boys at 58.32%, MSM at 27.94%, and transgender women at 32.59%, representing variation of at least 40 percentage points between highest and lowest coverage groups.
datoms.source: N. Ravishankar, Dr Sasidharanpillai Sabeena "Gender inequities regarding the HPV vaccination coverage in high-income countries: a systematic review and meta-analysis" (2025). doi:10.1101/2025.03.03.25323234
datoms.population: Adolescent girls, adolescent boys, men having sex with men (MSM), and transgender women aged up to 26 years in high-income countries
datoms.domain: Epidemiology and public health vaccination surveillance
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage variation between population groups (percentage point difference)
datoms.methodology: Systematic review and meta-analysis
datoms.sample_size: 2,998,403 total participants across 23 studies (1,975,415 girls, 804,882 boys, 11,909 MSM, 207 transgender women)
datoms.notes: Significant gender inequities exist in HPV vaccination coverage in high-income countries. Persistently high coverage was observed among adolescent girls, while HPV vaccination coverage was suboptimal among adolescent boys, MSM, and transgender women. The major barriers were low awareness among healthcare providers, lack of recommendations from clinicians, and public mistrust towards vaccines. Limitations: Most studies were cross-sectional, preventing adjustment for confounding factors. Studies on transgender women and MSM were all from the USA, limiting generalizability. Small sample sizes for transgender women resulted in wider confidence intervals. Self-reporting of vaccination status generated recall and social desirability bias.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies between different regions or administrative areas within a defined geographic jurisdiction during the early years of program implementation.
datoms.source: Émilien Jeannot, Philippe Sudre, Philippe Chastonay "HPV vaccination coverage within 3 years of program launching (2008–2011) at Geneva State, Switzerland" (2012). doi:10.1007/s00038-012-0352-2
datoms.population: University-age and catch-up-eligible populations in Geneva State, Switzerland
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage by region
datoms.methodology: Epidemiological surveillance study
datoms.notes: Regional variation in HPV vaccination coverage reflects differences in program implementation, healthcare access, and population acceptance across administrative areas within Geneva State. Limitations: Study limited to Geneva State; findings may not generalize to other Swiss cantons or countries with different healthcare systems or vaccination policies.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination final-dose coverage varies substantially by country income level, with low- and middle-income countries showing worse final-dose coverage than high-income countries due to higher dropout rates between first and final doses.
datoms.source: Laia Bruni, Anna Saura‐Lázaro, Alexandra Montoliu, María Brotons, Laia Alemany "HPV vaccination introduction worldwide and WHO and UNICEF estimates of national HPV immunization coverage 2010–2019" (2020). doi:10.1016/j.ypmed.2020.106399
datoms.population: Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and high-income countries with HPV vaccination programs
datoms.domain: Public health epidemiology and immunization policy
datoms.methodology: WHO/UNICEF epidemiological surveillance and coverage estimation
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage (first dose and final dose) stratified by country income level
datoms.notes: The authors attribute the higher dropout in LMICs to implementation challenges and note that improving program performance in these settings is critical for meeting global elimination targets. Limitations: The paper does not provide specific quantitative comparisons of final-dose coverage between LMICs and high-income countries, limiting precision of the income-level variation estimate.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies substantially by WHO region, with the Americas and Europe showing the highest program introduction rates (85% and 77% of countries respectively) compared to other regions.
datoms.source: Laia Bruni, Anna Saura‐Lázaro, Alexandra Montoliu, María Brotons, Laia Alemany "HPV vaccination introduction worldwide and WHO and UNICEF estimates of national HPV immunization coverage 2010–2019" (2020). doi:10.1016/j.ypmed.2020.106399
datoms.population: WHO Member States stratified by WHO region (Americas, Europe, Africa, Eastern Mediterranean, Southeast Asia, Western Pacific)
datoms.domain: Public health epidemiology and immunization policy
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination program introduction rate by WHO region
datoms.methodology: WHO/UNICEF epidemiological surveillance and coverage estimation
datoms.notes: The authors highlight that while introduction rates are highest in the Americas and Europe, further expansion is needed in other regions, particularly among populous countries in low- and middle-income settings. Limitations: The paper does not provide detailed breakdown of introduction rates for all WHO regions, limiting assessment of variation across all regions.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies geographically, with school-based vaccination reducing healthcare access-driven territorial disparities between regions with high and low general practitioner access.
datoms.source: Aurélie Bocquier, Morgane Michel, Judith E Mueller, Maïa Simon, Amandine Gagneux-Brunon "One-year impact on HPV vaccination coverage of a school- and primary care-based intervention: the PrevHPV cluster randomised trial." (2026). doi:10.1038/s41598-026-48222-x
datoms.population: 11-14-year-olds in French municipalities stratified by general practitioner access
datoms.domain: Public health, vaccination policy, health equity
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage variation by healthcare access and geographic region
datoms.methodology: Cluster randomized trial with post-hoc subgroup analysis
datoms.notes: School-based vaccination may reduce healthcare access-driven territorial disparities in HPV coverage by providing vaccination in settings accessible to all adolescents regardless of GP availability. Limitations: Post-hoc analysis; specific percentage-point variation between highest and lowest coverage regions not quantified in the paper.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies significantly between rural and urban regions in central Illinois, with a measurable percentage-point difference in coverage rates.
datoms.source: Eric Adjei Boakye, Yuri Fedorovich, Megan White, Sameer Vohra, Meredith Volle "Rural-Urban Disparities in HPV Vaccination Coverage Among Adolescents in the Central Part of the State of Illinois, USA" (2022). doi:10.1007/s10900-022-01136-x
datoms.population: Adolescents in central Illinois, USA
datoms.domain: Public health epidemiology; vaccine coverage surveillance
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage rates by rural vs. urban region
datoms.methodology: Cross-sectional epidemiological survey
datoms.notes: The authors interpret rural-urban disparities as reflecting differences in healthcare access, provider availability, or vaccination promotion efforts between geographic areas. Limitations: The specific magnitude of disparities, absolute coverage percentages, and comparison to national public-health targets are not provided in the available text excerpt.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage among girls aged 16–17 years in catch-up cohorts varies significantly by area-level deprivation, with coverage in the least deprived quintile (42%) exceeding that in the most deprived quintile (27%), a difference of 15 percentage points.
datoms.source: A. Hughes, D. Mesher, Joanne White, K. Soldan "Coverage of the English national human papillomavirus (HPV) immunisation programme among 12 to 17 year-old females by area-level deprivation score, England, 2008 to 2011." (2014). doi:10.2807/1560-7917.ES2014.19.2.20677
datoms.population: Girls aged 16–17 years offered catch-up HPV immunisation in England, 2008–2010; 151 Primary Care Trusts
datoms.measure: Three-dose HPV vaccination coverage by area-level deprivation quintile
datoms.methodology: Ecological analysis with Spearman rank correlation
datoms.notes: The authors conclude that school-based delivery at age 12 achieves equitable coverage, but catch-up cohorts aged 16+ show concerning inequality. The association with deprivation emerges around age 16, when compulsory full-time education ends in England. This may reflect reduced accessibility to school-based sessions or increased opting-out in older ages. Limitations: Area-level deprivation does not apply uniformly to all residents within an area. Individual-level factors associated with coverage were not assessed. Data recording may have been less complete for older girls vaccinated by GPs. The observed association could reflect either lower uptake or incomplete recording in deprived areas.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage in adolescent girls varies substantially across countries, ranging from several percent to more than 90%.
datoms.source: Barbara Owsianka, Maria Gańczak "Evaluation of human papilloma virus (HPV) vaccination strategies and vaccination coverage in adolescent girls worldwide." (2015)
datoms.population: Adolescent girls worldwide
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage rates (%)
datoms.methodology: Literature review and comparative analysis
datoms.notes: Disparities in HPV vaccination coverage rates worldwide may be due to different strategies of vaccination implementation between countries. School-based administration with national funding appears associated with higher coverage rates. Limitations: Study limited to literature review period 2006-2014; specific quantitative variation between highest and lowest regions not explicitly quantified in all cases.

datoms.claim: Among unvaccinated adolescents, 82.5% had at least one missed HPV vaccination opportunity, indicating that achievable coverage could reach 94.8% if vaccination opportunities were not missed.
datoms.source: S. Meyer, David Nmn Yankey, Laurie D. Elam-Evans, S. Pingali, Shannon Stokley "P-5. Human Papillomavirus Vaccination Coverage Among Girls and Boys in the United States: A Birth Year Cohort Analysis of the National Immunization Survey-Teen, 2016–2022" (2025). doi:10.1093/ofid/ofae631.216
datoms.population: Unvaccinated adolescents born 1999–2009 in the United States
datoms.measure: Missed HPV vaccination opportunities and achievable coverage
datoms.methodology: Birth cohort analysis using National Immunization Survey-Teen
datoms.notes: Opportunities for HPV vaccination before age 13 years are being missed and can be reduced by effective provider recommendations for HPV vaccination and by administering all recommended vaccines during the same visit. Limitations: The study analyzed data from 2016 to 2022 and focused on birth cohorts 1999–2009. NIS-Teen is a telephone survey which may have response bias.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination series completion among U.S. adolescents aged 13–17 years remained below the Healthy People 2030 target of 80% during 2021–2023, with completion rates ranging from 62.4% to 63.9%.
datoms.source: Taylor Mullin, Jesse Plascak, Alai Tan, Jodi Ford, Henry Duah "Trends in HPV vaccination initiation and completion among U.S. adolescents aged 13-17 years, 2021-2023: Findings from the National Immunization Survey-Teen." (2026). doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0349299
datoms.population: U.S. adolescents aged 13–17 years (n=126,226)
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination series completion rate (%)
datoms.methodology: Repeated cross-sectional survey analysis with provider-verified vaccination records
datoms.notes: HPV vaccine series completion among U.S. adolescents remained stable from 2021 through 2023, with overall completion estimates ranging from approximately 62% to 64%. Despite this stability, substantial gaps in HPV vaccination persist. Approximately one in five adolescents remained unvaccinated each year, and an additional one in seven initiated the vaccine series without completing it. Limitations: HPV vaccination estimates derived from public-use NIS-Teen dataset may differ from CDC's annual MMWR publications due to lack of internal harmonized dose-validation variables and total survey error adjustments. Only three years of data analyzed, limiting ability to infer long-term trends. Study was descriptive and did not examine sociodemographic or contextual predictors of uptake.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies substantially between girls and boys, with girls' coverage reaching 73.4% and boys' coverage reaching 65.9% among the 2009 birth cohort.
datoms.source: S. Meyer, David Nmn Yankey, Laurie D. Elam-Evans, S. Pingali, Shannon Stokley "P-5. Human Papillomavirus Vaccination Coverage Among Girls and Boys in the United States: A Birth Year Cohort Analysis of the National Immunization Survey-Teen, 2016–2022" (2025). doi:10.1093/ofid/ofae631.216
datoms.population: Girls and boys born 1999–2009 in the United States
datoms.methodology: Birth cohort analysis using National Immunization Survey-Teen
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage stratified by sex
datoms.notes: Coverage with on-time HPV vaccination increased by birth cohort among adolescents born 1999–2009 but remains suboptimal, with persistent sex-based disparities. Limitations: The study analyzed data from 2016 to 2022 and focused on birth cohorts 1999–2009. NIS-Teen is a telephone survey which may have response bias.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination completion rates vary by insurance type, with patients having private insurance 4% more likely to complete the vaccine series than those with Medicaid.
datoms.source: L. Khalil, E. Russo, K. Venkatakrishnan, A. Mazul, J. Zevallos "Barriers to Human Papillomavirus Vaccination Initiation and Completion among Adults Aged 18–26 Years in a Large Healthcare System" (2023). doi:10.3390/cancers15174243
datoms.population: Adults aged 18–26 years with at least one encounter at UPMC between 2018 and 2021
datoms.domain: Epidemiology and public health vaccination surveillance
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination completion rate by insurance type (percentage completing full 3-dose series)
datoms.methodology: Cross-sectional retrospective study with Poisson regression
datoms.notes: The authors note that an association was found between insurance type and HPV vaccination status. Patients with private insurance were found to be more prone to complete HPV vaccination than those with either Medicaid or another insurance type. The exact reasons underlying the observed differences in HPV vaccine uptake across various insurance coverages remain uncertain, and further investigation is necessary. Limitations: Cross-sectional design prevents causal inference. Study limited to UPMC patients in one healthcare system. HPV status subject to recall bias from clinical intake forms, though validation showed high concordance.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage among university-age and catch-up-eligible populations in Japan remains below public-health targets, with the highest cumulative vaccination rate at 33.6% for first dose among the FY2006 birth cohort as of June 2023.
datoms.source: Mahiro Sazawa, Chieko Ishiguro, W. Mimura, M. Maeda, Fumiko Murata "Impact of the resumption of proactive recommendation of HPV vaccination on HPV vaccination rates in Japan: an interrupted time series analysis based on the VENUS study" (2025). doi:10.1136/bmjph-2024-000982
datoms.population: Girls born between fiscal years 2003–2011 eligible for routine HPV vaccination in one Japanese municipality
datoms.domain: Epidemiological surveillance and vaccination policy implementation
datoms.methodology: Interrupted time series analysis with segmented Poisson regression
datoms.measure: Cumulative HPV vaccination rates (first, second, and third doses) among female birth cohorts
datoms.notes: The resumption of proactive recommendation promoted HPV vaccinations; however, the changes in vaccination rates remain insufficient compared with WHO targets. Additional efforts are required to encourage and promote vaccination in the Japanese population. Limitations: Data from a single municipality in Japan; generalizability to other regions not assessed. Study period limited to January 2019–June 2023.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage among boys aged 13-17 varies by rural-urban residence, with boys from isolated small rural towns showing lower initiation (17.3%) and completion (5.31%) rates compared to urban boys (28.7% and 10.7% respectively), representing a 11.4 percentage point difference in initiation.
datoms.source: Allison L. Swiecki‐Sikora, Kevin Henry, Deanna Kepka "HPV Vaccination Coverage Among US Teens Across the Rural‐Urban Continuum" (2019). doi:10.1111/jrh.12353
datoms.population: US boys aged 13-17 years stratified by rural-urban residence
datoms.methodology: Cross-sectional survey analysis with logistic regression
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination initiation (≥1 dose) and completion (≥3 doses) rates by geographic region
datoms.notes: Rural boys experience substantially lower HPV vaccination coverage than urban boys. Geographic disparities may reflect differences in healthcare access, provider recommendations, or awareness of HPV vaccination benefits for males. Limitations: Cross-sectional design limits causal inference. Data from 2012-2013 may not reflect current coverage. ZIP code-based classification may not perfectly capture individual rural-urban status.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage for full-dose completion among girls aged 9-14 years is 47.6% (95% CI: 39.7%-57.4%), substantially below the 90% public-health target.
datoms.source: Han Jingjing, Li Zhang, Yuqing Chen, Yuelun Zhang, Le Wang "Global HPV vaccination programs and coverage rates: a systematic review" (2025). doi:10.1016/j.eclinm.2025.103290
datoms.population: Girls aged 9-14 years across 129 WHO member states
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage rate (full dose completion)
datoms.methodology: Systematic review with meta-analysis
datoms.notes: The substantial gap between full-dose coverage (47.6%) and first-dose coverage (61.6%) indicates significant dropout between doses, highlighting the need for strategies to improve vaccination completion rates. Limitations: Not explicitly stated in the provided text.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage varies by jurisdiction, with differences ranging up to 48.4 percentage points for up-to-date status across selected state and local areas.
datoms.source: Laurie D. Elam–Evans, David Yankey, James A. Singleton, Natalie Sterrett, Lauri E. Markowitz "National, Regional, State, and Selected Local Area Vaccination Coverage Among Adolescents Aged 13–17 Years — United States, 2019" (2020). doi:10.15585/mmwr.mm6933a1
datoms.population: Adolescents aged 13–17 years across 50 states, District of Columbia, and selected local areas
datoms.measure: HPV up-to-date vaccination coverage by jurisdiction
datoms.methodology: National cross-sectional survey with jurisdiction-level stratification
datoms.notes: The authors emphasize that disparities in coverage across jurisdictions indicate that not all adolescents are equally protected against vaccine-preventable diseases, highlighting the need for targeted interventions in lower-coverage areas. Limitations: Jurisdiction-level estimates may have wider confidence intervals and lower reliability than national estimates due to smaller sample sizes within some jurisdictions.

datoms.claim: HPV vaccination coverage rate in France is 17.2% in girls aged 16 years, which is substantially lower than the 70% coverage rate observed in other Western European countries.
datoms.source: M. Uhart, Marjorie Adam, André Dahlab, Xavier Bresse "Loss of chance associated with sub-optimal HPV vaccination coverage rate in France" (2017). doi:10.1016/j.pvr.2017.02.004
datoms.population: Girls aged 16 years in France and Western Europe
datoms.measure: HPV vaccination coverage rate (percentage of girls vaccinated)
datoms.methodology: Epidemiological surveillance and policy documentation review
datoms.notes: The authors note that differences in HPV vaccination program implementation and coverage rates may lead to a two-tiered Europe, contributing to health inequality and representing a missed opportunity for thousands of individuals who will not be protected against vaccine-preventable cancers. Limitations: The vaccination coverage rate data were based on 2014-2015 figures; the distribution of vaccinees among cohorts and by year were not fully characterized due to lack of detailed data.

scope: Teens and young adults, ages 9 to 26, in the US, Belgium, France, Switzerland, Australia, and across Europe more broadly.
metric: How many people got the HPV vaccine and finished the full series, measured in percent, and how much coverage differs from one region to another, measured in percentage points.
aboutClaim:
This claim is based on 196 real sources, 145 of which support it and 51 of which say it depends on the situation, with zero sources disagreeing outright. Yet it still only scores 20 out of 100, which we call Speculative. That gap isn't because the studies disagree, it's about the quality and completeness of the evidence.

68% of the sources are based only on abstracts, short summaries, rather than the full published study. The methods used across the 196 sources are described 123 different ways. And the claim itself has a blank spot, an unfilled "[X] percentage points" gap, so no single, agreed-upon coverage-gap number exists across the studies.

The overall finding, that coverage falls short of targets with big regional differences, like the 54-61 point gap between Flanders and Wallonia-Brussels, shows up almost everywhere in the sources. But none of this evidence has been checked by a human reviewer yet.
